The Grass-eater (Distichodus rostratus) is a robust characiform fish native to the freshwater systems of West Africa, where it attains a considerable ultimate standard length of 76 cm [Li = 76 cm]. This species is notable for its strong pharyngeal dentition adapted for processing a predominantly herbivorous diet of aquatic macrophytes and detritus. Hatchlings emerge from eggs with a remarkably small wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00088 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00088 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 1.19 mm typical for the genus. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-eclosion, and the transition to exogenous feeding occurs once the mouth opens and the yolk is fully resorbed. Field studies conducted in the Niger River basin indicate that this initial mass is consistent across populations, though slight variations correlate with maternal size and local nutrient availability during gonadal maturation.

During the prolonged juvenile growth phase, Distichodus rostratus undergoes a gradual trajectory toward reproductive maturity, with puberty occurring at a standard length of 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm]. At this developmental milestone, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 360 grams [Wwp = approximately 360 grams], representing a substantial 400,000-fold increase from the neonatal mass. This pronounced somatic investment is necessary before the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis activates, initiating vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. The relatively large size at first reproduction is an advantageous life-history strategy in the variable floodplain habitats the species occupies, as larger individuals are better able to withstand seasonal fluctuations in water level and food availability. Congeneric species show similar allometric relationships, though the specific length-weight scaling exponent in D. rostratus, derived from extensive field collections, yields a robust power-law relationship linking length to mass across the entire size range.

The maximum reproductive output of Distichodus rostratus under optimal thermal conditions is considerable, reflecting the species' iteroparous spawning strategy. At a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], females produce approximately 12,004 eggs per kilogram of body mass [N_R_i = 12,004 eggs per kilogram of body mass], and with a mean adult female mass near 5,900 grams, a single spawning event can involve over 70,000 eggs. The spawning frequency is estimated at roughly 1.9 spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly 1.9 spawning events per year], which together with the fecundity per event yields a sustained annual reproductive output matched to the seasonal productivity pulse of the West African hydrological cycle. This reproductive rate is temperature-dependent, with the 28 °C [T = 28 °C] regime reflecting the mean annual water temperature in the species' core range. The buoyant, non-adhesive eggs are broadcast into the water column during seasonal flood peaks, ensuring optimal dispersal and oxygenation for the developing embryos.

The ultimate wet weight of 5,900 grams [Wwi = 5,900 grams] recorded for large adult Distichodus rostratus is attained only after many years of sustained growth in productive habitats such as the lower Niger delta and Lake Chad basin. This asymptotic mass corresponds closely to the 76 cm [Li = 76 cm] maximum standard length through the species-specific length-weight relationship, a scaling pattern that is shared among other large-bodied Distichodus species though the absolute values differ. Individuals reaching this upper size class are typically females over ten years of age that have accumulated substantial lipid reserves in their coelomic cavity, which are mobilized during successive reproductive cycles. The growth trajectory slows markedly after puberty, as energetic resources are increasingly diverted toward gamete production rather than somatic expansion, a common pattern among iteroparous teleosts. Old, gravid females approaching the asymptotic mass are a prized catch in artisanal fisheries and are increasingly rare due to size-selective harvesting pressure across much of the species' range.

Regarding the species' longevity, the maximum lifespan of Distichodus rostratus maintained under controlled conditions at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] has been documented at approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years], a duration derived from both captive observations and otolith-based age estimation from wild-caught individuals. This comparatively long lifespan for a characiform of this size is likely linked to the relatively stable thermal regime and predictable seasonal food resources in the species' native floodplain habitats. Senescent individuals show characteristic signs of physiological decline, including reduced gonadal output and diminished feeding efficiency, before eventual natural mortality. The interplay between the 28 °C [T = 28 °C] thermal regime and the 9-year (9 years) [am = 9 years] lifespan suggests a metabolic pace that is slow relative to smaller, more short-lived characins, and aligns with broader life-history predictions linking body size and temperature to longevity in tropical freshwater fishes.
